stances.claim: Moral turpitude is generally understood as 'an act contrary to justice, modesty, or good morals; an act of baseness, vileness or depravity in the private and social duties which a man owes his fellowmen.'
Macatangay v. CSC (June 15, 2022, J Hernando) correctly held bigamy to be moral turpitude warranting dismissal of a DFA employee -- an easy decision to agree with.

Republic v. Marcos II (Aug 4, 2009, J Peralta) -- distinguishing false return, fraudulent return with intent to evade, and failure to file ITRs, and holding only the first two to involve moral turpitude -- is harder to agree with; the cryptic and strained explanation may even draw rage, but it remains the prevailing jurisprudence and all of us are duty-bound to follow it while working to reverse, modify, or clarify it.

Buenafe v. Comelec (June 28, 2022, J Zalameda, en banc) affirmed and reiterated Republic v. Marcos II, distinguishing tax evasion (fraud through pretenses and forbidden devices) from negligent failure to file (not immoral, not depraved).

With due respect, the Court should have engaged petitioners' request to 'reexamine the totality of circumstances' -- to add flavor to the already-meaty ponencia and to explain why a lowly DFA employee is dismissed while a candidate with 31,629,783 votes is treated differently.

But the Court has spoken; we all have a duty to follow -- 'to undo an election, there must be compelling and unequivocal evidence of the candidate's disqualification,' and Marcos Jr.'s COC contains 'no false material representation.'

notable_anecdotes: The deliberate juxtaposition of ALL-CAPS section openers -- 'DISMISSAL FROM EMPLOYMENT WAS THE ANSWER OF THE SUPREME COURT' (easy to agree) and 'IT MAY NOT BE EASY TO AGREE WITH THIS DECISION' (Marcos II) -- making the column's structural critique itself typographic.
CJ's verdict on the Marcos II reasoning -- 'cryptic and strained explanation' -- one of the sharpest editorial adjective-pairs in the late columns about a sitting doctrine.
The lowly-DFA-employee-vs-31.6M-voter contrast as the central justice asymmetry -- CJ does not name the unfairness explicitly but the structural pairing renders it unmistakable.

The duty-to-follow doctrine articulated as a civic discipline: 'as long as the ruling is not reversed, or modified, or clarified to be merely an obiter dictum... it is the prevailing jurisprudence and all of us are duty-bound to follow it, while working to reverse or modify or clarify it.'
The compliment-with-criticism move -- 'low profile Justice Rodil V. Zalameda' and 'the already meaty ponencia' -- preserving respect for the ponente while disputing the result.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the doctrine of moral turpitude through three Supreme Court decisions. In Macatangay v. CSC (June 15, 2022), penned by Justice Ramon Paul I. Hernando (First Division), the Court ruled that bigamy is a crime involving moral turpitude and consequently dismissed a Department of Foreign Affairs employee convicted of it -- a decision easy to agree with. In Republic v. Marcos II (Aug 4, 2009), penned by Justice (later CJ) Diosdado M. Peralta (Third Division), the Court held that Ferdinand Marcos II's failure to file ITRs for 1982-1985 was not moral turpitude -- distinguishing false returns, fraudulent returns with intent to evade, and mere failure to file, and treating only the first two as involving the requisite 'willfulness and fraudulent intent.' This decision, CJ concedes, is harder to agree with -- some may rage against its 'cryptic and strained' explanation -- but it is the prevailing jurisprudence and all are duty-bound to follow it 'while working to reverse or modify or clarify it.' Instead of reversal, however, the en banc in Buenafe v. Comelec (June 28, 2022), penned by 'low profile' Justice Rodil V. Zalameda, affirmed and reiterated it -- clarifying that tax evasion involves fraud through pretenses and forbidden devices while negligent failure to file is 'not of itself immoral.' The Court brushed aside petitioners' request to 'reexamine the totality of circumstances,' which CJ -- with due respect -- believes it should have engaged, if only to explain why a lowly DFA employee is dismissed for bigamy while a presidential candidate who 'gathered 31,629,783 votes, or 58.77%' is treated differently. 'But the Court has spoken' -- and to undo an election requires compelling and unequivocal evidence the COC simply does not bear.
